phase1.title: Your CamperDNA
phase1.subtitle: 15 questions. Personalised spec in your inbox.

questions.question: What's your total budget for the van and any conversion work?
questions.helper: This covers everything — the base van plus any conversion costs. It's the master filter for everything else.

options.label: Under £20,000

questions.question: How are you planning to buy?
questions.helper: Each route produces a completely different report — inspection advice, converter selection, or self-build guidance.

options.label: Buy a pre-converted van (already fitted out by someone else)
Buy a donor van and commission a conversion company
Buy a donor van and self-build (or partial self-build)
Not decided yet

questions.question: Which generation are you considering — or not sure yet?
questions.helper: This affects emissions compliance, platform, conversion ecosystem, and long-term running cost.

expand.body:
T6.1 (2019+) is fully Euro 6 and ULEZ-compliant. T6 (2015–2019) requires checking — models built from September 2016 onwards are Euro 6 compliant, but earlier T6s and some late 2016 vans were still Euro 5. Always verify using the TfL ULEZ checker or the V5C before buying. T5 (Euro 5) is not ULEZ-compliant — attracts daily charges in London, Bath, Bristol, Birmingham and a growing list of others. T5 offers more van for the money if you never drive into these zones.

T7 Transporter (unveiled 2024, UK deliveries from mid-2026) is a completely different vehicle — co-developed with Ford on the Transit Custom platform. UK orders open Spring 2026. Available with diesel, PHEV, and electric powertrains. The conversion ecosystem (roof kits, RIB beds, furniture profiles) built around T5/T6/T6.1 doesn't carry over. There are no established conversion templates and virtually no converter experience on the platform yet. Only worth considering if you're buying in late 2026 or beyond and want a brand-new van.

options.label: T6 / T6.1 (2015 or newer) — Euro 6 compliant, widest conversion ecosystem
T5 (2009–2015) — excellent reliability, better value, not ULEZ-compliant
T7 Transporter (UK from mid-2026) — new platform, barely arrived, no conversion ecosystem yet
Not sure — help me understand the differences

questions.question: How do you feel about buying a higher-mileage van?
questions.helper: Service history matters far more than the number on the clock.

expand.summary: Why service history matters more than mileage
expand.body: A T6 TDI with 140,000 miles and a complete VW stamped service history is a better buy than a 60,000 mile van with gaps. These engines are proven at high mileage when properly maintained. Under 50K is rare below £40K — be realistic about what your budget allows.

options.label: Under 50,000 miles — better resale, more years ahead
Happy with 100–150,000 with full service history — much better value
Depends on price and history

questions.question: Where are you planning to buy the base van?
questions.helper: Each source has different guarantees, processes, and price implications.

expand.body: VW Approved Used: 12-month warranty + 115-point inspection including bodywork. Wales & North of England tends to have cheapest stock. Private sale: budget £250–400 for an independent inspection — always worth it. Via conversion company: convenient and they know what makes a good donor, but their markup is often built into the conversion quote.

options.label: VW Approved Used (12-month warranty, 115-point check — recommended)
Private sale (better prices, less comeback if something goes wrong)
Conversion company sourcing it (convenient, they know what to look for)
Not sure yet

questions.question: If buying a T6 donor, what trim level are you targeting?
questions.helper: One decision that's very hard and expensive to fix later.

expand.body: Aircon is essentially impossible to retrofit economically (£1,500–2,500+). The Highline includes it as standard, plus heated front windscreen (genuinely useful for camping mornings) and front/rear parking sensors. The price premium at base van level is nearly always smaller than the retrofit cost. Always buy the Highline if you can.

options.label: Highline (recommended — aircon standard, heated windscreen, parking sensors)

Sportline (lifestyle grade above Highline — 204PS DSG, lowered sports suspension, premium interior. Note: lowered suspension is a disadvantage for campsites and rough tracks; interior gets stripped in a conversion so the premium may not be worth it)
Trendline or Startline (budget — aircon often missing, needs retrofitting)
Already have a van / not applicable

questions.question: What gearbox are you looking for?
questions.helper: This affects price, engine availability, and day-to-day driving feel — especially on urban routes and for towing.

expand.body: DSG (7-speed dual-clutch automatic) first appeared on the T5.1 facelift in September 2009 — a world first for a medium van at the time. Available on 150PS and 204PS engines only; the 102PS entry engine comes with a 5-speed manual only. Most conversion buyers choose between 6-speed manual (150PS) and DSG (150PS or 204PS). DSG adds roughly £1,500–2,500 to the purchase price but makes stop-start urban driving and towing significantly smoother. Note: DSG on older T5 units (pre-2012) has a mixed reliability record — check service history carefully.

options.label: 6-speed manual — most common, reliable, lower purchase price (available with 150PS and 204PS engines)
7-speed DSG automatic — smoother in traffic and towing, higher purchase price (150PS or 204PS only)
5-speed manual — older T5 or 102PS engine, lowest cost, very reliable
Not decided yet

questions.question: How many seats do you need in the back of the van?
questions.helper: This affects bed width, storage, and kitchen space — more than most people expect.

expand.body: 3 front seats and 2 rear is the right default. Going to 3 rear costs more to convert, narrows the bed by ~10cm, and significantly reduces storage and kitchen space. Unless you genuinely need to seat 3 children in the back, the 2-rear layout is better in almost every way.

options.label: 2 rear seats (recommended — wider bed, more kitchen and storage space)
3 rear seats (ISOfix for three children, but loses storage)
Not sure

questions.question: Barn doors or tailgate?
questions.helper: This affects bike rack compatibility and day-to-day family use more than anything else.

expand.body: Barn doors: easier for families, compatible with towbar bike racks that swing open around them, no problem if someone parks close behind you. Tailgate: provides rain shelter when open, slightly cleaner look, easier single-handed loading. Summary: barn doors for families, either works for couples or solo.

options.label: Barn doors (two doors opening sideways)
Tailgate (single door lifting upward)
Not sure — explain the difference

questions.question: What roof setup do you want?
questions.helper: Affects headroom, cost, whether you can use multi-storey car parks, and extra sleeping space.

expand.body: Pop-top: sweet spot for most buyers — extra sleeping space without losing multi-storey car park access (stays under 2m). Only consider quality-tested roofs — these maintain body integrity. High-roof: maximum headroom, mechanically simple, but taller driving profile and some car parks become inaccessible. Standard/Day Van: lowest cost, accept that you'll always be changing at a slight crouch.

options.label: Pop-top (elevating roof — extra sleeping, stays under 2m for car parks)
High-roof (fixed raised — full standing height, no mechanism to maintain)
Standard roof (no modification — lowest cost, limited headroom)

questions.question: What's your priority for the main sleeping area?
questions.helper: Each option involves real trade-offs between crash safety, comfort, and boot space.

expand.body:
RIB Altair (recommended for families): purpose-designed as a travel seat first, bed second. Available in 2-seat (112cm wide — the most common choice) and 3-seat (129cm wide) versions. Note: the 3-seat version significantly reduces the space available for kitchen units. Pull-tested to ECE R14 (M1 standard), meaning car seats can be legally fitted. ISOfix is standard. Raises up to create usable boot storage underneath.

Rock and Roll bed: traditional fold-flat rear bench. Simpler and cheaper. Budget versions are not M1 crash-tested (car seats cannot legally be fitted). Premium options — Reimo Variostar, Rusty Lee — are now also M1 pull-tested and offer ISOfix. Worth specifying a premium unit if children will travel in the van.

Fixed bed: always made up but eats into boot space — best if you never need the boot for large items (bikes, boards, buggies).

options.label: RIB bed (folds from rear seat — ISOfix points, crash tested, storage underneath)
Rock and Roll bed (fold-flat — simple, widely available)
Fixed bed (always made up — maximum convenience, less boot space)
Not sure

questions.question: What do you mainly do outdoors?
questions.helper: This drives rack, storage, and accessory spec — gets this right at conversion time rather than retrofitting.

options.label: Surfing or water sports (board storage, roof rack, rinse shower)
Cycling or mountain biking (bike rack essential)
Hiking, climbing or trail running (lighter gear, less storage intensive)
General use — no specific sport or large kit

questions.question: Do you want external shelter attached to the van?
questions.helper: These are very different products serving very different needs.

expand.body: Retractable awning: extends out in seconds for shade and light rain cover — great for impromptu stops. Awning rail: a track on the van's side that lets you pitch a drive-away tent which stays when you drive off — useful for families who want the van for sleeping but extra space for the kids.

options.label: Retractable awning (extends out for shade and light rain cover)
Awning rail (rail on van side — drive-away tent slots in and stays when you drive off)
No awning needed

questions.question: Do you need a diesel night heater?
questions.helper: Year-round use is transformative — but not essential for summer-only camping.

expand.body: ~£1,000 fitted as part of a conversion. Draws from the van's fuel tank. Runs quietly on 3–5 amps. Phone-controllable with the right controller — you can warm the van before you get up. If your partner is coming, this is usually the dealbreaker. Specify at conversion time — retrofitting is messier and pricier.

options.label: Yes — year-round use, cold nights, want to warm the van remotely
Probably — but not sure what's involved
No — mainly summer use, campsites with electricity

questions.question: How important is it to camp without a mains hookup?
questions.helper: This determines your solar panel and battery spec — decisions that need to happen at conversion time.

expand.body:
A solar panel and leisure battery (~£600 fitted as part of a conversion) means you're generating and storing your own power — so you're not dependent on a hookup at all.

This matters in more situations than just wild camping. If you're joining friends who are tent camping, there's no hookup option on a standard grass pitch — you either have power or you don't. And on campsites that do offer hookup, it typically costs £5–10 extra per night and usually puts you on a hard-standing pitch rather than grass. For families who want a softer, quieter spot, that's often not ideal.

A well-specified system (100–200W panel, 100Ah lithium battery) will comfortably run LED lighting, a compressor fridge, phone charging, and a diesel heater fan for several days without sun. It won't run a kettle or hair dryer — those need hookup or a separate inverter.

The key reason to decide now: solar requires cutting a hole in the roof and running cables during the build. Retrofitting after the van is finished means disturbing the ceiling lining, re-routing cables, and paying for labour twice. Specify it at conversion time.

options.label: Essential — I want to wild camp and never rely on campsites
Useful — mix of wild camping and campsites
Not important — I'll mostly use sites with electric hookup

phase2.title: Full Conversion Spec
phase2.subtitle: Build your brief. Take it to a conversion company.
phase2.description: Tick everything you want included. Each section is independent — skip any that don't apply. When you're done, we'll send your spec sheet to the same email address you used in the questionnaire.

emailLogic.note: If the user completed Phase 1, their email is stored in sessionStorage under 'camperdna_email'. Phase 2 should check for this on load. If found, show a confirmation line ('We'll send your spec to [email] — not you? Update below') with an optional override field. If not found, show a required email input field before allowing submission.

sections.title: Roof
sections.helper: The roof choice affects headroom, sleeping capacity, driving profile, and whether you can access multi-storey car parks. Decide this early — it affects the rest of the conversion.

items.label: Standard roof
items.helper: No modification to the factory roof. Lowest cost option. Limited headroom — you'll always be at a slight crouch inside. Fine if budget is tight.

items.label: Pop-top roof
items.helper: A hinged roof section that lifts to create extra headroom and sleeping space above the main van. Stays under 2m when closed so multi-storey car parks remain accessible. Usually includes a sleeping platform and canvas sides. Quality matters — specify a tested unit.

items.label: High-roof (fixed raised)
items.helper: A permanently raised fibreglass or steel roof giving full standing height throughout the van. Mechanically simple (no mechanism to maintain). Taller driving profile — some car parks and ferries become inaccessible. Popular with full-time van lifers.

sections.title: Roof Extras
sections.helper: Additional roof features beyond the basic structure.

items.label: Electric ventilation fan
items.helper: An electrically powered roof fan that extracts cooking smells and condensation. Can also run in reverse to push air in. Far better than a passive vent. Usually 12v, draws 3–5 amps.

items.label: Skylight / roof light (non-opening)
items.helper: A fixed clear or smoked acrylic panel in the roof that admits natural light. Cheaper than a fan, no moving parts, but no ventilation benefit.

items.label: Roof rack
items.helper: Load-carrying rack on top of the van. Useful for surfboards, kayaks, ladders, or additional storage. Check compatibility with your roof choice — not all pop-tops accept a roof rack on top. Raises driving height.

sections.title: Sleeping
sections.helper: The bed configuration is one of the most important decisions — it affects crash safety (especially if children are travelling), boot storage, and day-to-day livability.

items.label: RIB bed (crash-tested, ISOfix points)
items.helper: A proprietary rear seat system that folds flat into a bed. Crash tested to M1 standard, which means car seats can be legally fitted. Raises up at an angle to create usable boot storage underneath. The recommended choice for families. Comes in various widths — specify at conversion time.

items.label: Rock and Roll bed
items.helper: A traditional fold-flat rear bench where the back hinges down to create a flat sleeping surface. Simple, robust, widely available second-hand. Not crash tested to M1 standard (car seats cannot be legally fitted). Works well for couples or solo use.

items.label: Fixed bed (always made up)
items.helper: A permanent bed that never needs folding. Maximum sleeping convenience — you can get straight in. Reduces boot/rear storage significantly. Best if you never need the boot for large items (bikes, boards, buggies).

items.label: Single / twin bed layout
items.helper: Two single beds, usually longitudinal (running front-to-back). Requires a wider van or specific layout. Common in larger campervans and motorhomes. Unusual in T5/T6 standard wheelbase.

items.label: Pop-top sleeping platform
items.helper: A platform in the elevated pop-top section. Usually fits one adult or two children. Includes a thin mattress that stays in the roof when collapsed. Requires a pop-top roof.

items.label: Mattress topper / comfort layer
items.helper: An additional foam layer on top of the main bed surface. The factory-spec bed foam is usually 50–75mm — fine for a night, noticeable after several. A good topper makes a meaningful difference. Specify one that folds with the bed.

items.label: Bed width: standard (~112cm)
items.helper: The standard RIB 2-seat / Rock and Roll width in a T5/T6. Comfortable for one adult, manageable for two.

items.label: Bed width: wide (~129cm — 3-seat RIB)
items.helper: The 3-seat RIB Altair configuration. Wider sleeping surface but significantly reduces the space available for kitchen units. Suitable if seating 3 in the rear is a priority.

items.label: Bed width: full-width (~150cm)
items.helper: Full van width, usually only achievable with a fixed bed or specific Rock and Roll configuration in a long-wheelbase van. Maximum sleeping comfort for two.

sections.title: Seating
sections.helper: Seating configuration affects living space, storage, and whether the van can legally carry the passengers you need.

items.label: 2-seat rear bench
items.helper: Two rear passenger seats. Recommended for most buyers — allows wider bed, more kitchen space, and more storage. Standard in most conversion layouts.

items.label: 3-seat rear bench
items.helper: Three rear passenger seats with three seatbelts. Allows seating for more passengers. Narrows the available living space and bed width. Usually required if carrying three children.

items.label: Swivel front seat (driver)
items.helper: The driver's cab seat rotates 180° to face the living area when parked. Creates a much more social layout — four people can sit facing each other around a table. Adds cost, requires a swivel base plate.

items.label: Swivel front seat (passenger)
items.helper: The double passenger cab seat rotates 180°. Usually done alongside the driver swivel for a full face-to-face seating configuration.

items.label: Captain seat (single front passenger)
items.helper: A single armchair-style seat in the front passenger position instead of a bench. More comfortable for long drives. Loses the option of seating a second front passenger.

items.label: Seat upholstery re-trim
items.helper: Recovering the cab and/or rear seats in a fabric or material of your choice to match the conversion interior. Usually done at conversion time — easier and cheaper than retrofitting.

items.label: ISOfix child seat points
items.helper: Factory ISOfix anchor points for child car seats. Confirm your bed system includes M1-rated ISOfix points — this is what allows legal child seat fitting on the bed/seat.

sections.title: Kitchen
sections.helper: How much kitchen you need depends entirely on how you camp. A simple hob and cold water tap suits most weekend users. A full fitted kitchen with fridge, hob, sink, and hot water is worth specifying if you use the van regularly.

items.label: No fitted kitchen
items.helper: No permanent cooking facilities. Relies on a portable camp stove and cool box. Lowest cost, maximum flexibility. Common in weekender/surf van conversions.

items.label: Single gas hob
items.helper: One gas burner/electric hob. Usually Gas runs from a small (907) gas bottle stored in a ventilated locker. Enough for boiling a kettle or basic cooking. Requires a dropout gas vent in the van body.

items.label: Twin gas hob
items.helper: Two gas burners/electric hobs — much more practical for cooking proper meals. Same gas supply and safety requirements as single hob. The standard for most fitted conversions.

items.label: Hob + sink combination unit
items.helper: A single unit combining a twin hob and sink in one worktop cutout. Space-efficient — the most common kitchen configuration in T5/T6 conversions. Saves ~200mm of worktop length versus separate units.

items.label: Cold water tap (electric pump)
items.helper: A 12v electric pump draws from the fresh water tank to the tap. Cold water only. Standard in most conversions. Fresh/grey water tank is usually 12–25 litres and located under the sink or in one of the storage units.

items.label: Hot and cold water
items.helper: Adds a water heater (usually 12v or gas-powered) to provide hot water at the tap. Adds cost and complexity. Worthwhile for longer trips or if a shower is included.

items.label: Compressor fridge (top-loading)
items.helper: A top-opening compressor fridge — the most energy-efficient option. Holds cold better when opened (cold air doesn't fall out). Usually 40–50L. More expensive than a front-loading fridge. Requires 12v power.

items.label: Compressor fridge (front-loading)
items.helper: A swing-door fridge that fits under the worktop like a standard kitchen fridge. Easier access than top-loading, slightly less efficient. Usually 40–50L. Requires 12v power.

items.label: Portable cool box (no fitted fridge)
items.helper: A removable 12v cool box rather than a fitted compressor fridge. Lower cost, more flexible, but less efficient and less convenient than a compressor fridge. Good for occasional/weekender use.

items.label: Gas bottle locker with dropout vent
items.helper: A dedicated sealed locker for the gas bottle with a vent that opens to outside the van. Required for any gas installation — gas must not be able to accumulate inside the van.

sections.title: Heating
sections.helper: Heating options range from none (summer use only) to a fully controllable diesel heater you can operate from your phone before getting out of bed.

items.label: No dedicated heating
items.helper: No fitted heater. Suitable for summer-only use or campsites with electric heating. You can always add a portable electric heater on hookup.

items.label: Diesel night heater
items.helper: Draws diesel from the van's main fuel tank — no separate fuel supply needed. Runs quietly, draws 3–5 amps from the leisure battery. Fully heats the van within 10–15 minutes. The standard choice for year-round use. Specify at conversion time — retrofitting is messy and more expensive.

items.label: Phone / app-controllable heater timer
items.helper: An additional controller that allows you to set temperature, schedule wake-up times, and control the heater from your phone. Works via Bluetooth or SIM card depending on the controller. Roughly £120–200 on top of the heater unit. Genuinely transforms the experience.

items.label: Gas heater
items.helper: A gas-fired heater fed from the van's gas bottle. Simple and cheap. Less efficient than diesel for van use — you're carrying a separate fuel supply. Requires gas safety certification.

sections.title: Electrics
sections.helper: The electrical system is what makes wild camping possible. Specify this carefully — retrofitting solar and wiring is the most disruptive and expensive post-conversion upgrade.

items.label: AGM leisure battery 100Ah
items.helper: Lead-acid AGM (absorbent glass mat) battery. 100Ah capacity but only ~50Ah usable before damaging the battery. Proven, widely serviced, lower upfront cost. 3–5 year lifespan. Fine for light use.

items.label: AGM leisure battery 200Ah+
items.helper: Larger AGM bank for more demanding use — fridge, diesel heater, lighting. Still limited to 50% depth of discharge. Heavy.

items.label: Lithium (LiFePO4) battery 100Ah
items.helper: Lithium iron phosphate battery. 100Ah fully usable (vs 50Ah for AGM of same rating). Lasts 2,000+ charge cycles. Half the weight of AGM. 3× higher upfront cost. The upgrade that makes off-grid van life genuinely comfortable. Recommended if you plan to keep the van.

items.label: Lithium (LiFePO4) battery 200Ah+
items.helper: 200Ah+ lithium bank for full off-grid capability — fridge, diesel heater, large inverter, multi-day no-sun operation. Serious capacity for serious use.

items.label: Split charge relay (basic alternator charging)
items.helper: A relay that connects the leisure battery to the van's alternator when the engine is running. Simple, cheap. Less efficient than a DC-DC charger — doesn't protect the starter battery as well under high load.

items.label: DC-DC charger (B2B charger — recommended)
items.helper: A smart battery-to-battery charger that efficiently charges the leisure battery from the alternator. Properly protects the starter battery. The correct choice for lithium batteries. Worth specifying over a basic split charge relay.

items.label: Solar panel 100W
items.helper: Entry-level solar. Keeps the battery topped up in summer. Unlikely to run a fridge in low sun. Good for light use — lighting, charging, diesel heater fan only.

items.label: Solar panel 200W
items.helper: Standard single-panel setup. Enough for most light off-grid use in UK spring/summer — fridge, lighting, phone charging, diesel heater. Usually two 100W panels wired in parallel.

items.label: Solar panel 400W+
items.helper: Full off-grid setup. Two 200W panels. Enough for year-round use including winter. Overkill for summer-only use, perfect if you use the van in autumn and winter.

items.label: MPPT solar charge controller
items.helper: Regulates the charge from solar panels into the battery. MPPT (Maximum Power Point Tracking) is more efficient than PWM — extracts up to 30% more power in low light. Bluetooth monitoring on quality units means you can see real-time solar input from your phone.

items.label: 240v mains hookup socket
items.helper: An external socket that accepts a campsite 'shore power' cable. Allows you to charge the leisure battery and run 240v appliances directly from campsite power. A 16-amp blue socket is standard.

items.label: 240v mains sockets (internal)
items.helper: Standard UK 3-pin sockets inside the van — powered via hookup or inverter. Useful for charging laptops, running appliances. Usually fitted near the kitchen or seating area.

items.label: 12v cigar-lighter sockets
items.helper: Standard 12v outlets for running 12v accessories — kettles, portable fans, etc.

items.label: USB sockets (A and/or C)
items.helper: Dedicated USB charging points. USB-C is increasingly important for modern phones, laptops, and headphones. Specify both A and C if possible.

items.label: Touchscreen power management panel
items.helper: A display panel that shows battery state, solar input, and controls leisure power circuits. Not essential but gives good visibility of your electrical system. Some systems allow remote monitoring via phone.

sections.title: Lighting
sections.helper: Lighting is often an afterthought but makes a significant difference to how liveable the van feels. All lighting should be LED and 12v — no exceptions.

items.label: LED ceiling spotlights
items.helper: Recessed or surface-mounted LED spotlights as the main van lighting. Usually 3–5 spots in a T5/T6. Wired to a switched circuit from the leisure battery.

items.label: Dimmable lighting
items.helper: A dimmer switch or dimmable LED drivers so ceiling lights can be set to any level. Particularly useful for evenings — harsh full brightness is uncomfortable in a small space.

items.label: Under-cupboard task lighting
items.helper: LED strip or small spots under the overhead lockers, above the kitchen worktop. Makes cooking and prep much easier in the evening.

items.label: Reading light over bed
items.helper: A directed light over the sleeping area for reading. Can be a small directional spot or a flexible neck light. Very useful — avoids disturbing a sleeping partner.

items.label: Ambient / mood LED strip
items.helper: LED strip lighting along the ceiling perimeter, under cabinets, or behind furniture for indirect ambient light. Creates atmosphere. Can be RGB/colour-changing or warm white only.

items.label: Pop-top interior light
items.helper: A light inside the pop-top sleeping area. Small LED light for the upper bunk area. Essential if children sleep up top.

items.label: Exterior step / door light
items.helper: A small LED light at the sliding door step — very useful at night when getting in and out. Low power draw, triggered by door opening.

sections.title: Storage
sections.helper: Storage in a van is never enough. Plan it carefully at conversion time — retrofitting shelves and drawers is easy, retrofitting an overhead locker rail or under-floor storage is not.

items.label: Overhead lockers (above hob/sink)
items.helper: Cupboards running along the upper walls of the van, above the hob/sink usually. Most valuable storage in the van for clothes, food, and light items. Usually 2–3 separate locker sections.

items.label: Overhead lockers rear (above bed)
items.helper: Shallow cupboards running across the rear of the van above the bed. Valuable extra storage for light items you can easily reach when in bed. Usually 2–3 separate locker sections.

items.label: Under-bed pull-out drawers
items.helper: Drawers that slide out from underneath the bed platform. Good for clothing, kitchen equipment, and items you need regular access to without lifting the bed. Stops items sliding around when driving.

items.label: Under-bed open storage (lift-up access)
items.helper: A lifting bed panel that reveals storage below — accessed less easily than drawers but gives a larger, more flexible storage area. Good for bulky or less-used items.

items.label: Wardrobe with hanging rail
items.helper: A tall locker with a rail for hanging clothes. Usually in the rear corner beside the bed. Useful for longer trips — keeps clothes uncrumpled.

items.label: Wardrobe with shelving
items.helper: A tall locker with fixed shelves instead of a hanging rail. More versatile for mixed items — folded clothes, shoes, equipment.

items.label: Kitchen rail / spice rack
items.helper: A mounted rail or small shelf in the kitchen area for frequently used items — bottles, spices, utensils. Small but makes kitchen use much more practical.

sections.title: Windows & Privacy
sections.helper: Privacy and blackout capability are essential for comfortable overnight stays. Condensation management (good ventilation + insulation) is equally important.

items.label: Opening side window
items.helper: A hinged or sliding window in the van's side wall usually above the hob so heat and cooking fumes can escape. Provides ventilation when parked. Usually added on one or both sides. Essential for hot weather.

items.label: Fixed tinted privacy windows
items.helper: Non-opening windows with dark tint (privacy glass). Allows light in while making it difficult to see in from outside. Often fitted on the non-opening side.

items.label: Roller blinds (window-fit)
items.helper: Slim roller blinds that fit precisely into each window aperture. Block light, provide privacy, reduce condensation. Neater than external covers but less effective as thermal insulation.

items.label: Pleated blinds
items.helper: Pleated fabric blinds that fold flat when not in use. Better thermal properties than roller blinds. Some systems provide both a sheer layer (daytime privacy) and a blackout layer.

items.label: Cab screen wrap / cover (driver + passenger)
items.helper: Covers for the two front cab windows. Essential for full blackout. Cheap options don't possess thermal qualities.

items.label: Cab divider / bulkhead curtain
items.helper: A curtain or panel between the cab and living area. Helps retain heat in the living area, improves privacy, and reduces condensation from the cab windows.

items.label: Full insulation lining (walls and ceiling)
items.helper: Closed-cell foam insulation applied to all van walls and ceiling, covered by a lining material (usually carpet or fabric). Significantly reduces condensation and improves heat retention. Should be standard in any quality conversion.

items.label: Acoustic insulation (sound deadening)
items.helper: Butyl rubber sound deadening sheets applied to the van panels before lining. Reduces road and engine noise considerably. Adds cost and a small amount of weight. Should be standard in any quality conversion.

sections.title: Exterior
sections.helper: Exterior fittings that affect day-to-day use, bike/board carrying, and campsite setup.

items.label: Barn doors (rear)
items.helper: Two rear doors opening sideways. Easier family access, compatible with swing-out towbar bike racks (bikes can remain in situ). Less issue with access if someone parks close behind you.

items.label: Tailgate (rear)
items.helper: A single door that lifts upward. Provides a rain canopy when open, and potential option for shower fitting. Slightly cleaner look. Any towbar rack works with a tailgate (the door opens upward, not sideways — but you will need to remove the bikes first).

items.label: Rear door window (glass insert)
items.helper: A glass window in the rear barn door or tailgate. Adds light to the interior, improves rearward visibility. Tinted versions available.

items.label: Retractable awning
items.helper: A permanently mounted awning on the van's roof rail that rolls out to provide 2–3m of canopy. Deploys quickly with no additional equipment needed. Great for shade and light rain cover.

items.label: Awning rail (for drive-away tent)
items.helper: An aluminium track bonded to the van's side wall. Compatible drive-away tents slot in and remain pitched when you drive off. More versatile for families wanting extra sleeping/living space on site.

items.label: Fold-down entry step
items.helper: A fold-down step at the sliding door opening. Lowers the step height into the van — useful for children and shorter adults. Some versions deploy automatically when the door opens.

items.label: Towbar (fixed)
items.helper: A permanent fixed towbar. Cheaper than detachable. Always visible when not in use. Compatible with bike racks and lightweight trailers. 13-pin electrics for trailer boards.

items.label: Towbar (detachable)
items.helper: A towbar with a removable neck — stows away when not needed. Cleaner appearance, higher cost. Useful if aesthetics matter and towing is occasional.

sections.title: Safety
sections.helper: Basic safety items that are required at many campsites and on some ferry crossings.

items.label: Fire extinguisher
items.helper: A small dry powder or CO2 extinguisher mounted accessibly near the door. Required for many campsites and some ferry crossings. 1kg minimum.

items.label: First aid kit
items.helper: A basic first aid kit mounted in an accessible location. Required for some campsites. Practical for any trip.

sections.title: Finish & Cosmetics
sections.helper: The finishing choices — furniture material, floor, and lining. These define how the van looks and feels. They're easier to change post-conversion than structural elements, but it's still worth deciding upfront.

items.label: Furniture finish: wood grain / natural effect
items.helper: Warm, classic look. Various wood species available — oak, walnut, birch are common. More traditional feel. Popular for family vans.

items.label: Furniture finish: gloss white
items.helper: Clean, modern look. Makes the interior feel larger and lighter. Shows marks more than wood. Popular for contemporary conversions.

items.label: Furniture finish: grey / slate
items.helper: Neutral, modern. Hides marks better than white. Versatile with most interior colours.

items.label: Furniture finish: bespoke / painted
items.helper: Custom colour match or painted furniture to a specific RAL or sample colour. Adds cost and lead time. For buyers who want a specific look.

items.label: Floor covering: vinyl / LVT
items.helper: Luxury vinyl tile or sheet vinyl. Waterproof, easy to clean, warm underfoot, available in many designs. The most practical choice for van use. Recommended.

items.label: Floor covering: rubber / checker plate
items.helper: Rubber or pressed aluminium checker plate. Extremely durable, easy to clean, very practical for working/surf vans where mud and sand are regular. Less comfortable underfoot.

items.label: Ceiling lining: fabric / carpet
items.helper: Fabric or carpet headlining on the ceiling. Warm, soft, reduces condensation noise. The standard finish for most conversions.

items.label: Wall lining: carpet
items.helper: Carpet covering the van's metal walls. Warm, reduces condensation noise, good acoustic properties. The standard for most quality conversions.

items.label: Wall lining: ply panels
items.helper: Smooth ply panels on the walls. Easier to clean than carpet, modern look, can be painted. Popular with builders going for a cleaner interior aesthetic.

sections.title: Nice to Haves
sections.helper: Accessories and aesthetic upgrades that aren't core to the conversion but make a meaningful difference to the look and daily experience. Most can be added after the conversion — though some are easier and cheaper to specify upfront.

items.label: Wireless Apple CarPlay / Android Auto
items.helper: T6.1 (2019+) Highline and above often includes CarPlay wired as standard — a wireless retrofit adapter (£40–80) removes the cable. Older T6 and T5 need a head unit replacement: a quality double-DIN unit with wireless CarPlay and Android Auto runs £250–450 fitted. One of the most practical upgrades for day-to-day use — navigation, music, and calls without touching your phone.

items.label: Side running boards
items.helper: Aluminium or steel steps mounted below the sliding door sill. Lower the step height into the van — useful for shorter adults and children. Some versions fold flat when not in use. Cost: £150–350 supply and fit depending on material and style. Check clearance if you use the van off-road or on rough tracks.

items.label: Body kit — front splitter
items.helper: A front lip spoiler fitted below the standard front bumper. Adds an aggressive, lowered look. Available in gloss black, carbon-effect ABS, or colour-coded to the van. Popular options from specialist suppliers including ABT Sportsline and Caractère. Cost: £200–600 supply and fit. Note: lowers the front ground clearance slightly — worth considering if you use the van on rough tracks or steep drives.

items.label: Body kit — rear spoiler
items.helper: A roof-mounted or tailgate spoiler in ABS plastic or fibreglass. Adds visual height and a sportier profile to the rear. Available in OE finish or colour-coded. Mainly aesthetic — marginal aerodynamic benefit in real-world van use. Easier to fit on a standard or high-roof than a pop-top. Cost: £180–500 supply and fit.

items.label: Alloy wheels
items.helper: T6 Highline includes alloys as standard (17"). T5 and lower-spec T6 vans often come on steel wheels with plastic trims. An alloy upgrade transforms the look considerably. Quality van-rated alloys from Keskin, BBS, or OZ in 17–18" typically cost £600–1,200 for a set of four including tyres. Stick to 17–18" for a loaded van — larger diameters reduce sidewall height and can be harsh on poorer road surfaces.

items.label: Reversing camera
items.helper: A rear-facing camera that feeds an image to the head unit or a dedicated screen when reversing. Extremely useful on a van — blind spots are significant. Can be mounted on the number plate, tailgate, or barn door handle. Works with most aftermarket CarPlay head units. T6.1 top-spec trims include a factory camera; T5 and most T6 need a retrofit. Cost: £150–350 supply and fit depending on integration with the head unit.

items.label: LED headlights
items.helper: T6.1 (2019+) includes LED daytime running lights as standard on most trims; full LED headlights on higher specs. T5 and T6 typically have halogen headlights — an LED upgrade makes a significant difference to night driving quality and gives the van a more modern, premium look. Direct-fit LED bulb replacements run £80–150; full LED headlight assemblies (better beam pattern and legality) run £400–700 supply and fit.
